questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following demarcates the anterior 2/3rds of the tongue from the posterior 1/3rd?
questions.explanation:
The anterior two-thirds of the tongue is demarcated from the posterior one-third by the terminal sulcus, also known as the sulcus terminalis.

Sulcus terminalis divides the tongue into anterior and posterior parts. The anterior or oral part faces superiorly and the posterior or pharyngeal part faces posteriorly.

Sigmoid sulcus is present on the mastoid surface of the temporal bone. Gingival sulcus is present between a tooth and the surrounding gingival tissue. Median sulcus is the central sulcus present on the tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the papillae marked A in the given image.
questions.explanation:
The structure marked A shows the foliate papillae, which lie bilaterally on either side of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis.

Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections mainly on the dorsal anterior two-thirds. Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, red papillae mainly on the lingual margins and dorsal surface. Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges present bilaterally near the sulcus terminalis. Circumvallate papillae are large cylindrical structures, around 8-12 in number, arranged in a V-shaped row immediately anterior to the sulcus terminalis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: All the following muscles of the tongue are derived from occipital myotomes except:
questions.explanation:
All the muscles of the tongue are derived from occipital myotomes except palatoglossus. Palatoglossus is derived from the fourth pharyngeal arch.

Accordingly, all tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus, which is supplied through the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: While examining the hypoglossal nerve in a stroke patient, you observe the following finding. Which of the following muscles is likely to be paralyzed?
questions.explanation:
The image shows deviation of the tongue to the left; the left genioglossus is paralyzed.

When both genioglossi contract they protrude the anterior tongue in the midline. When one contracts, it protrudes and pushes the tongue to the opposite side. Genioglossus also depresses the central tongue and is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.

With hypoglossal nerve palsy, the ipsilateral genioglossus is paralyzed and the protruded tongue deviates toward the affected side because of unopposed contraction on the normal side.

Genioglossus is attached to the genial tubercle and helps prevent the tongue from falling backward and obstructing respiration; the source notes this as the safety muscle of the tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient who underwent skull base surgery developed drooping of the left side of his face and loss of taste sensation in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. However, the general sensation over the tongue is intact. Which of the following nerves is likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
The clinical picture indicates facial nerve damage above the stylomastoid foramen with involvement of the chorda tympani.

Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by chorda tympani, whereas general sensation is carried by the lingual nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: While testing the taste sensation in a stroke patient, you place a few drops of sugar water over the circumvallate papillae. Which of the following nerves will carry the taste pathway here?
questions.explanation:
Taste from the circumvallate papillae is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, except the circumvallate papillae, is carried by chorda tympani. Glossopharyngeal innervation includes the circumvallate papillae, posterior one-third of the tongue, palatoglossal arches, and oropharynx.

Taste buds in the extreme posterior tongue and epiglottis receive fibres from the internal laryngeal branch of the vagus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with a painful aphthous ulcer at the tip of the tongue. Which of the following nerves gives rise to the branch carrying this sensation?
questions.explanation: Pain sensation at the tip of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve, which is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.structuredExplanationText: Pain sensation at the tip of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve, which is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 50-year-old man with a history of tobacco chewing presented with a painless ulcer over the tip of the tongue. Wedge biopsy revealed squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following lymph nodes would you first biopsy?
questions.explanation:
The submental lymph node is biopsied first because it is the sentinel node for lesions at the tip of the tongue.

In squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue, submental nodes are involved in lesions of the tip, whereas submandibular nodes are involved in lesions of the lateral tongue. Bilateral neck-node spread is common because lymphatic vessels cross the midline.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient with long-standing erythroplakia now presents with the following finding. Which of the following lymph nodes would be involved first in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The image shows carcinoma involving the marginal part of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Lymphatics from this region drain first to unilateral submandibular lymph nodes.

All lymphatics from the tongue ultimately drain into deep cervical nodes along the internal jugular vein; the jugulo-omohyoid nodes are therefore described as lymph nodes of the tongue.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: You notice the following finding while administering OPV for a child. Which of the following nerves does not provide sensory supply to the structure involved?
questions.explanation:
The image shows a cleft palate. Sensory supply to the palate is not provided by the hypoglossal nerve, which is a pure motor nerve.

General sensation from most of the soft palate is carried by the lesser palatine nerve (V2), pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve, and the plexus around the tonsil. Taste from the oral surface of the soft palate is carried by the lesser palatine nerve; taste fibres initially travel in the greater petrosal nerve, a branch of the facial nerve, and traverse the pterygopalatine ganglion without synapsing.

All muscles of the soft palate are supplied through the pharyngeal plexus (CN X) except tensor veli palatini, which is supplied by the mandibular nerve. The hard palate is supplied by the greater palatine and nasopalatine branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The sensory fibers from the taste buds in the hard and soft palate travel along the _______.
questions.explanation:
The sensory fibres from taste buds in the hard and soft palate travel along the trigeminal nerve.

Taste from the oral surface of the soft palate is carried by the lesser palatine nerve. The taste fibres initially travel in the greater petrosal nerve, a branch of the facial nerve, and pass through the pterygopalatine ganglion without synapsing.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following does not supply the palate?
questions.explanation:
The tonsillar branch of the facial artery supplies the palatine tonsil and not the palate.

The hard palate is supplied by the greater (descending) palatine artery, a branch of the third part of the maxillary artery. The soft palate is supplied by the ascending palatine branch of the facial artery, the ascending pharyngeal artery, and lesser palatine arteries.
